summary: Mostly stage 1: good handbook, training and budget, but person-dependent, topic choice ad hoc, conflicts unpublished, no update policy.

sources.title: Garner 2015 - Estonia guideline programme, interim appraisal (WHO Europe)

evidence.text: Programme rests on the insurance fund's mandate to pay for quality care (p. 4); no guideline law cited

1.1.missing: Any law or decree naming guidelines

evidence.text: National handbook since 2011 after a two-year preparation; 2015 updates (pp. 1, 13)
Insurance fund coordinates with 2 full-time staff; Guideline Advisory Board selects topics (pp. 4, 6)
Industry influence suspected on one guideline's questions; reviewers urge refusing commercial funding (pp. 6, 11)
"Driven by highly energetic and committed individuals"; nearly stalled when two staff left (pp. 5, vi)
Societies and University of Tartu involved; nurses and patients hard to include (pp. 1, 5)
Reviewers ask the government to "demonstrate political commitment" and state the value in health policy (pp. vii, 12)
Under half a million euros over about five years, mostly the insurance fund; ministry paid for 2 public-health guidelines (p. 4)
No industry funding reported; reviewers recommend a ban (p. 11)
One coordinator; reviewers advise contracting Tartu or the national institute, ideally "more than one contracted group" (p. 11)
Board decisions "seem to be based on the committee's opinions on the day" (p. 9)
Mostly bottom-up proposals from clinicians and specialist societies (pp. 6, 11)
No evidence summary per proposal; reviewers suggest one (p. 9)
Board named, composition not given
Asthma and cardiovascular topics fit burden, but no statin guideline despite high cardiovascular mortality (p. 6)
Alcohol guideline arose from a research institute's funding (p. 6)
Secretariat skills of two staff "a major contributor" (p. vi)

4.1.missing: Number of people able to lead

evidence.text: Capacity "spread throughout different organizations" (p. 10)

4.2.missing: Number able to deliver end to end

evidence.text: Evidence-to-decision frameworks not used; patient input weak (pp. 7-8)
Annual training since 2010; over 200 clinicians trained; no recognition for panel time (pp. 1, 5, 6)
15 guidelines in progress, 3-5 complete in five years; "low turnover" (pp. 1, 4)
Handbook valued; adoption and adaptation "needed further development" (p. 5)
Secretariat "diligent in searching for existing guidelines and evidence" (p. 7)
Reviewers recommend using health-services utilisation data (p. 11)
Surgical safety checklist adopted; adaptation option in the handbook not used (pp. 6, 11)
Three guidelines appraised with AGREE once, by the review; weak link from evidence to recommendation (pp. 6-7)
No update policy; reviewers propose a three-year check (p. 13)
Handbook requires declarations and publication (p. 7)
Trial funding from drug companies noted; secretariat judgements not documented (p. 7)
Guidelines public; declarations not published (p. 7)
Rejected proposers get no feedback (p. 9)
The payer runs the programme, but the link to reimbursement "needs explicit consideration" (p. 12)
Expensive medicines in guidelines flagged as a problem; explicit policy recommended (p. 12)
Clinical indicators and audit run separately; reviewers urge linking them (p. 12)
Each completed guideline has an implementation plan, mostly education (p. 12)
Small, centralised system
Uptake "perceived to be low"; unclear if guidelines are mandatory (pp. 1, 8)
Icons and summaries; Russian versions and mobile formats requested (p. 9)
Survey of 586 health workers on barriers (Annex 5)
Senior specialists see guidelines as a threat; "small country dilemma" (p. 8)
Clinical indicators exist but not tied to guidelines (p. 12)
Effects expected "over the next few years" (p. vi)
This WHO appraisal, plus the 2010 assessment (pp. 1-2)
2010 assessment produced the handbook; this review drives its update (pp. 1, 13)

assessedByNote: Desk score by the CERC team from an external WHO appraisal
